title: Smile at the Reception Desk

briefing.headline: Aftersales in a car dealership group: what you should know before the call
points: A family-owned group of five dealerships for one car brand in Brussels and Walloon Brabant, selling new cars and running workshops for servicing and repairs.
Service advisors take bookings, receive customers at the desk, explain the work and the invoice, and hand the car back.
The brand importer phones a sample of customers after each workshop visit and publishes a customer satisfaction index (CSI) per dealer.
Part of the dealer's margin from the importer is variable and linked to standards such as CSI.
Mechanics and advisors fall under the joint committee for the metal and motor trade; staff work in French and Dutch.

stakeholder.name: Philippe Delcourt
stakeholder.org: Groupe Delcourt-Verbist SA, five dealerships of one brand with 14 service advisors and about 60 mechanics
stakeholder.voice: Charming salesman turned manager, switches between French and Dutch mid-sentence. Speaks in percentages and anecdotes about 'a client last week'. Proud of the commercial results of aftersales. Gets slippery when pay or the owner's family comes up.

frontline.name: Stijn Lambrechts
frontline.role: Service advisor at the Waterloo branch, eight years in
frontline.voice: Friendly, fast-talking, half an eye on the queue at the desk. Bilingual. Defends his colleagues, blunt about the workshop planning.

opening_message: Bonjour. The importer's CSI came in: we are second to last in the region on aftersales. Second to last. It costs us the quarterly margin bonus, about 90,000 euro across the group. My service advisors need a customer service training. Welcome, smile, empathy, the full thing. Fourteen people, five sites. Can you have something before the next survey wave in November?
surface_ask: A customer service and friendliness training for 14 service advisors.

gold.real_problem: Customers are unhappy about cars not ready at the promised time and invoices higher than the quote, not about how they are welcomed. The advisors already know how to promise a realistic time and call for approval before extra work: they do it on Saturday mornings and in August, when the desk is quiet, and the one site that books with a buffer scores near the regional average. On weekdays the system pushes them the other way: advisors must book the workshop at 100% of mechanic hours, the workshop chef plans separately on a whiteboard, and the advisor bonus pays for extra labour hours added at the desk with no condition on customer approval. Philippe designed that bonus and the 100% booking target, and the workshop reports to the owner's son, not to him.
gold.need_statement: The group does not need advisor training. It needs workshop booking with a buffer for unplanned work, one shared plan between advisors and the workshop chef, and an advisor bonus that pays for approved extra work and cars ready on time instead of surprises on the invoice. L&D's role is to say no to the smile course, put the CSI and dealer-system evidence in front of Philippe and Olivier together, help them design and run a one-site pilot of the new booking routine, and help explain the bonus change to the advisors.

hidden_facts.fact: On the CSI questions about welcome and friendliness the group scores above the regional average. It scores far below on 'vehicle ready at the promised time' and 'invoice matched the estimate'.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks which CSI questions are low, what the survey actually measures, or for the detailed report.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The detail? Well, the welcome is fine, friendliness is fine. It's the... ready on time, the invoice. But the customer is grumpy at the desk, so it's the desk, non?
hidden_facts.data_doc: Aftersales CSI by item, group vs region (0-100). Welcome at reception 88 vs 84. Friendliness of advisor 86 vs 83. Explanation of work done 71 vs 78. Vehicle ready at promised time 52 vs 76. Invoice in line with estimate 49 vs 74. Overall 63 vs 78.
hidden_facts.data_source: Importer CSI report, last two quarters

hidden_facts.fact: Advisors are told to book the workshop in the dealer system at 100% of mechanic hours, a target Philippe set, leaving no room for unplanned repairs, absences or waiting for parts. The workshop chef ignores the system and plans on his own whiteboard, so promised times are missed several times a day. The advisors know a full book means a late afternoon; they book it full because that is the target.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how workshop appointments are planned, how a pick-up time is promised, or how advisors and the workshop work together.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: We book in the system, yes. The workshop... has its own way. It's always been a bit like that.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: I know how to promise a time, I've done it eight years. But I book the system full, because full is the target. Then Marcel in the workshop plans on his whiteboard, his way. One car waits for a part, the whole afternoon shifts. At four I'm on the phone saying sorry fifteen times. Then they get the survey.

hidden_facts.fact: Since last year advisors get a monthly bonus on extra labour hours sold at the desk, with no condition on customer approval. They add brake pads, wiper blades and air-conditioning service during the visit, often without calling the customer first, because a call costs time and a 'no' costs bonus. That delays the car and inflates the invoice.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how advisors are paid or targeted, what drives extra work on the invoice, or why invoices exceed the estimate.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: There is a small bonus on additional hours sold. It's commercial, that's the job. Aftersales revenue is up 11%, by the way. I designed it myself.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Service advisor variable pay: 4% of extra labour hours sold above the original booking, paid monthly. No condition on customer approval or CSI. Introduced January last year.

hidden_facts.fact: On Saturday mornings and in the August holiday weeks, when the desks are quiet and the booking target is not chased, the same 14 advisors hand back over 90% of cars on time and nearly every invoice matches the estimate. The skill is there; the weekday system works against it.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether the problem is the same every day or every season, whether some days or weeks go well, or for on-time and invoice figures by day.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Saturdays? Saturdays are calm, of course it goes well. That's not real life, that's a Saturday.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Dealer system extract, all five sites, last six months. Cars handed back at promised time: weekdays 58%, Saturday mornings 93%, August weeks 91%. Invoices within 10% of estimate: weekdays 51%, Saturday mornings 94%, August weeks 89%. Workshop booked as % of mechanic hours: weekdays 100%, Saturday mornings 70%, August weeks 75%. Extra labour hours added at the desk per car: weekdays 1.4, Saturday mornings 0.3.
hidden_facts.data_source: Dealer management system, hand-over and invoice report

hidden_facts.fact: At the Wavre site the advisor Nadia Lefèvre and her workshop chef ignore the 100% target: they book at about 80%, hold a short talk at the whiteboard every morning, and she phones every customer before adding work. Wavre's CSI on 'ready on time' and 'invoice matched estimate' is near the regional average. Nadia earns the lowest bonus in the group and got a remark in her appraisal about 'under-booking'. Nobody trained her; she just refuses to make promises the workshop can't keep.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether any site or advisor does better, who the best advisor is, or how the sites differ.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Wavre is... better, yes. Nadia. She is a bit stubborn, she books under the target. Her bonus is the smallest, so she is not exactly an example. But the customers like her, c'est vrai.
hidden_facts.data_doc: CSI by site, 'vehicle ready at promised time' / 'invoice in line with estimate' (region: 76 / 74). Waterloo 48 / 45. Brussels 46 / 44. Nivelles 51 / 47. Ottignies 50 / 49. Wavre 73 / 72. Advisor bonus paid last year, average per advisor: Wavre lowest of the five sites.
hidden_facts.data_source: Importer CSI report per site, with advisor variable pay totals

hidden_facts.fact: The workshops report to Olivier Verbist, the owner's son and Operations Director, not to Philippe. The two disagree about who owns customer promises and barely speak.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks who manages the workshop, who would need to agree, or who else is involved.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The workshops are Olivier's. Olivier is the son of Monsieur Verbist. We have... a respectful relationship. We greet each other at the New Year reception.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Aftersales Director (P. Delcourt): service advisors, parts counters. Operations Director (O. Verbist): workshops, workshop chefs, mechanics. Both report to the managing director (J. Verbist).

hidden_facts.fact: Last spring advisors were told to tell customers 'you may get a call, anything below 9 counts as a failure for us'. The importer noticed score begging at another dealer and sent a warning letter to all dealers.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what was tried before to raise CSI, or how advisors talk about the survey with customers.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: We tried a little... awareness. Advisors mentioned the survey. Then the importer sent a letter to everyone about 'influencing'. Not addressed to us. Not only to us.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Last spring we had to say 'only a 9 or a 10 counts'. Customers laughed at us. Then the importer sent a letter and we had to stop. Now we just pray.

volunteered_facts: The group is second to last in the region on the importer's aftersales CSI.
Missing the CSI standard costs about 90,000 euro of margin bonus per quarter across the group.
The advisors are experienced; most have been at the desk for years. 'They know the cars. It's the attitude.'

constraints.budget: About 25,000 euro this year, plus training credits the importer offers dealers through its own training centre.
constraints.deadline: Next importer survey wave starts in November, about seven weeks away.
constraints.audience: 14 service advisors on five sites; the workshop chefs and mechanics report elsewhere.
constraints.schedule: Desks open 7:30 to 18:00; advisors cannot all leave the same day. Saturday mornings are open at two sites.
constraints.languages: French at three sites, Dutch at one, mixed at the Brussels site.
data_available: Importer CSI report per site and per question
Dealer management system: bookings, promised times, actual hand-over times, estimates and invoices
data_not_available: Customer comments per advisor (the importer only reports per site)

dependencies.concern: Owns the workshops and their planning; sees aftersales as 'the people who overbook my mechanics'.
dependencies.if_ignored: Advisors learn to promise better times that the workshop does not keep.

dependencies.concern: Likes the revenue growth from the upsell bonus and the family peace.
dependencies.if_ignored: Any change to pay or planning gets parked 'until after the season'.

dependencies.concern: Owns the CSI survey, the bonus rules and the dealer training centre; watching for score begging.
dependencies.if_ignored: A clever fix to the score turns into another warning letter.

dependencies.concern: Changing the advisor variable pay touches individual contracts and the company's collective agreement.
dependencies.if_ignored: Fourteen advisors hear 'your bonus is going' and the desks get even less friendly.

traps: Overall CSI alone: one number, sampled, quarterly, influenced by everything.
Happy sheets or completion rates after a friendliness training nobody needed.
Mystery shopping of the welcome, which is already the strongest item.

gold_plan.baseline: Share of cars handed back at the promised time and share of invoices within 10% of the estimate, per site and per weekday versus Saturday, from the dealer system.
gold_plan.behaviour: Workshop booked at the agreed buffer, one shared plan used by advisor and chef, and recorded customer approval before any extra work, checked in the job card notes.
gold_plan.leading_indicators: Daily on-time hand-over rate; weekday booking level as % of mechanic hours; share of extra work with recorded customer approval.
gold_plan.business_metric: CSI items 'ready on time' and 'invoice matched estimate', and the quarterly margin bonus, weighed against aftersales revenue.
gold_plan.collection: Weekly dealer system report per site, pilot site against the others, importer CSI per quarter.

concepts.conventional: A customer service and friendliness training for all 14 advisors.
concepts.solid: No training. Recommend booking at about 80% of capacity, one shared plan between advisors and the workshop chef, an approval call before any extra work, and a bonus that counts only approved extra hours and includes on-time hand-over. Offer L&D's help where it fits: facilitating the sessions where Philippe and Olivier agree the routine, running the pilot and its measurement, and the briefing to advisors on the new bonus.
next_level_examples: Pilot at one site with Olivier as co-owner, copying Wavre: a ten-minute morning stand-up between advisors and the workshop chef at the whiteboard, which becomes the single plan. Nadia explains to the other sites how she does it, as a peer, not as a trainer.
Rebuild the advisor bonus on two measures, approved extra hours and cars ready on time, so selling and keeping promises pay the same, and take the 'under-booking' remark out of Nadia's appraisal.
Spend the importer training credits on a workshop-planning module that chefs and advisors attend together, framed as a process change rather than advisor training.
also_valid: Redirecting the 25,000 euro budget to facilitation, the pilot and a dealer-system report, with a clear written 'no' to the smile course and the evidence behind it.
red_flags: Friendliness or smile training as the main answer.
Training advisors to promise realistic times or call for approval, when they already do it whenever the target lets them.
Ignoring the upsell bonus or the 100% booking target because Philippe designed them.
Asking advisors to coach customers on the survey again.
Leaving the workshop and Olivier out of the plan.

defence_objections: No training at all? I have a budget, I have the importer's credits, and I have a director who wants to see that I did something. 'We changed a bonus' is not a programme.
Touch the bonus? Aftersales revenue is up 11% thanks to that bonus. The managing director will ask me why I am breaking the only thing that works.
Book at 80%? That's 20% of my mechanics' hours I am throwing away. Who pays for that?
You want me to go to Olivier and say his whiteboard should run my desk? Bon. You come with me.
question_you_didnt_ask: Is there a site, an advisor or a day of the week where this goes well, and what is different there?
actor_notes: Philippe is friendly and talkative but steers every answer back to 'attitude at the desk'. He reveals the bonus only when asked directly about advisor pay or targets, and then defends it with the revenue figure. He presents the 100% booking target as 'just good management'.

Asked about Wavre or the best advisor, he admits Nadia does better but frames her as stubborn and under-performing on bonus. He does not connect her results to the target or the bonus until the player does.
He becomes evasive and very polite about Olivier and the owner's family. A player who proposes involving Olivier as co-owner rather than as the culprit earns trust.
He respects players who ask for the detailed CSI report or the dealer-system figures; it is a little embarrassing that he never opened the CSI report past page one.
A clear 'no, training won't fix this' first annoys him, then relieves him if it comes with evidence and a concrete plan he can show the managing director.
If the player delivers the smile training, he is delighted, and the judge should note the missed diagnosis.
flavour_lines: Our advisors smile. They smile a lot at four o'clock, when they phone to say the car is not ready.
The importer sends us a coffee machine standard. Sixty pages. The coffee is excellent. The cars are late.

second_request.opening_message: Nobody signs up for our maintenance contracts. I want a sales technique course for the 14 service advisors.
second_request.after_right: The advisors phone customers when a job runs late, and the complaints halved. The owner noticed. So: new problem, and you get first go.
second_request.after_wrong: They smile beautifully now. The cars are still late. Let us try again, on something else.
second_request.need_statement: Customers who want a maintenance contract at the desk cannot sign one there, because the form needs the sales manager's signature and he is in the showroom only in the afternoon.
second_request.real_problem: Customers ask about the contracts often enough. The contract is a six-page importer form that must be countersigned by the sales manager, who works in the showroom in the afternoons, while most cars are dropped off before nine. The desk shows the importer's list price, which is higher than the group's own offer in the showroom. At Wavre, where the sales manager starts at eight, sign-ups are at the regional level.

hidden_facts.fact: The contract form needs the sales manager's signature, and he is only in from the afternoon, while most customers drop their car before nine.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: asks what happens when a customer says yes at the desk
hidden_facts.reveal_line: They cannot sign it at the desk. The sales manager countersigns. He comes in after lunch, the customers come in at eight.

hidden_facts.fact: The desk shows the importer's list price for the contract; the showroom offers the group's own, cheaper price.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: asks about the price or what customers are told
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The desk has the importer's price list. The showroom has ours. Ours is cheaper. Do not ask me why.

hidden_facts.fact: At Wavre, where the sales manager starts at eight, contract sign-ups are at the regional average.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: asks whether any site does better
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Wavre sells them, funnily enough. Their sales manager is an early bird.

second_request.question_you_didnt_ask: What happens, step by step, when a customer at the desk says yes?
